title: the Markandeya
tomorrow: what's the strangest thing a mother could sing to a baby?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Markandeya, and Harishchandra: an honored king and an angry sage, kept side by side. Today, the same Purana, and a part of it that's meant to be heard.

A friend drops you, and weeks later you're still checking what they post. In the Markandeya Purana, two men meet in a forest with that exact problem. King Suratha has lost his kingdom to enemies and to his own ministers. The merchant Samadhi has been thrown out by his own wife and sons, for his money. Neither can stop worrying about the people who did it. Is my treasury safe? Are my sons well? They know it makes no sense. So they ask the sage Medhas why.
screen: `STILL CHECKING THEIR POSTS.` → `A KING AND A MERCHANT, BOTH BETRAYED.` → `WHY CAN'T WE STOP CARING?`

segments.voice: Medhas's answer opens the Devi Mahatmya, the glory of the Goddess, a long section set inside the Markandeya Purana. Even the wise, he says, are drawn into clinging by the Goddess as Mahamaya, the great power that holds the world together, and when she's pleased, the same power sets a person free. Then he tells them her stories: battles against demons the gods couldn't beat. This is a text that lives in the ear. Some families and temples recite it whole during Navaratri, the nine nights of the Goddess, and some keep the recording playing all through those mornings. Its best-known hymn is built from one repeated shape. To the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness, and the line closes: namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah. Bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again. Then the same line again, with a new word: as sleep, as hunger, as patience, as mother. And one surprise in the list: bhranti, error, confusion, the very thing troubling the two men. The refrain doesn't argue. It just keeps bowing. At the end of the story, the king asks for his kingdom back, and the merchant asks for the knowledge that sets him free of mine.
screen: `EVEN THE WISE ARE DRAWN IN.` · `A TEXT THAT LIVES IN THE EAR.` · `NAMAS TASYAI: BOW TO HER.` · `EVEN AS CONFUSION.` · then, large: `THE SAME POWER SETS FREE.`

segments.voice: Find one steady sound near you: a fan, traffic, the hum of a fridge, your own breathing. Listen to it the way someone listens to a long recitation, not to understand it, just to stay with it. When your mind slides off toward someone you're worried about, notice, and come back to the sound.
The Markandeya. The Purana that holds the Devi Mahatmya, which opens with two men who can't stop caring.
Hold onto this: the Markandeya, where the power that binds is the power that frees. More tomorrow.
